title: What is in the seventh book of the Cesti
english: Table of contents. These things are in the seventh book of Africanus's Cesti: 1. On arming. 2. On the destruction of enemies. 3. On athletic contest. 4. For the cutting of one who has been struck. 5. For a wound from iron. 6. Taming a horse. 7. That a horse may not neigh. 8. For a horse's cataract. 9. That a horse may not be startled. 10. On the speed of horses. 11. The horse-frightener. 12. For the destruction of pack-animals. 13. For a kicking mule. 14. Military hunting. 15. To find the breadth of a river and the height of a wall. 16. Theft of sound. 17. A means of staying awake. 18. For a fight against elephants. 19. Paradoxes of farming. 20. A seal concerning the missile.
translator_notes: Greek locked from PG 10 / Khazarzar Cesti fragmenta, book 7 pinax. Restorations in angle brackets are in the lock (book-number zeta; wall-height). One numeral before horse-taming is blank in the lock; the list is otherwise 1-20.
No public-domain English of the Cesti body exists; ANF has the letters only.

title: Outcomes come by reason, law, fate, or chance
english: Proem. The issues of affairs — births and destructions, alterations and healings — come by reason, or by law, or by fate, or by chance. It is good to know each of these, gathering from them all a varied profit that bears fruit: a therapy of sufferings, or a hidden history, or beauty of speech. These things, in what has gone before and in what follows, have been achieved, as I think, according to my own modest measure.
translator_notes: Greek locked from PG 10 / Khazarzar Cesti book 7 proem. Restoration ἰάματ<α> is in the lock.

title: Heavy Greek panoply, not numbers, turns the fight
english: On arming. It is a good thing, in all matters, to know war as well. I have often wondered at the cause of the differing turn of armed contests, and from this that Greeks have beaten Romans, and Persians have beaten Greeks, and yet the Persians have not yet been beaten by the Romans, but the nations of upper Asia dare to claim freedom and force an equal rank toward us.

Giving an account to myself, I found the cause was not superiority of stratagems, nor soldierly strength as a whole (for among good men numbers count for nothing in war), but the preparation of the weapons and the form of the war-dress.

The Greeks delight in a heavy panoply: a double felt cap, a scale breastplate, a hollow bronze-faced shield held by two grips — one about the forearm, enough for shoving, the other held by the end of the hand — two greaves, a javelin in the hands, a close-fighting spear equal to that of the royal horsemen, and a broad sword that is not long. With this arming a run is rare: not far, but sharp, and only so much as a man pressing on needs in order to get inside missile-range in time.

They also knew how to lock shields together, and each of them fought on his own, so that the soldier's virtue was double: in common and alone. They used to cut down the barbarians in this way: they rested themselves often on the march, so that eagerness would not be blunted by the length of the road, and so they stayed fresh in this manner up to the dangers. Then, using sharp speed to get inside the missiles, they had work to do, the missiles flying farther over them once they had run in under the fall, while the others, because the infantry fought lightly armed, could not endure the charge of such a fence. For the power of a missile is length; at close quarters the safety of the fight is accomplished by the panoply.

So, that they may suffer nothing from afar, the breastplate is stronger than every missile by the folding of the scales, that it may remain unwounded; and the felt about the head, having a cap, and another overlay of bronze, and one helmet upon another, answers the shots from a sling, the outer scale being crushed and yielding so that what is sent may not reach the inner covering of the head. The face is bare and the neck free, so that looking round in every direction goes unhindered.

With the spears some hold off the lance-bearing horsemen, striking first before they fall on; others, setting their phalanxes more openly and opening a way, reach the barbarians. They also use peltasts and slingers without danger, screened in front by the wall of the arms. The short swords are useful for ease and for the violence of the blow. The Macedonian successors altered few of these things, because of the variety of their wars, and fitted out an arming common both against barbarians and against one another.
translator_notes: Greek locked from PG 10 / Khazarzar Cesti 7.1 On arming. This slice ends at the Macedonian successors; the lock-file remainder continues in u01-rem.
Bracketed Greek ὅπη δεῖ ἐλλεβοροστρῶσαι in the lock is left unrendered as a suspected interpolation; no English was invented for it.

title: Alexander’s cap, the shaved beard, and the Roman kit
english: A sign that the fighters' faces were left free under a Laconian felt cap in the Macedonian arming: they call this thing, and this practice, the soldier-king's. Alexander himself ordered the soldiers to shave their beards, and when someone rebuked him for shearing off the ornament of the face, he said: "You do not know, you unmilitary man, that there is no more convenient grip in a fight than a beard." Coming to close quarters with this arming, no barbarian would hold out, however he was equipped.

The Romans have a helmet of a single material, leaving the faces a little open for breath and sight, reaching down to the shoulder-blades, and tightening the neck so that it cannot turn; a chain-mail breastplate; one greave; a long sword; and a rectangular shield carried as a screen by the end of the hand. In the locking of shields this is weaker for the body, because the soldier cannot throw his whole shoulder into the weapon. Their spears are shorter than the Greek.

They fight with success against the panoply already described. They have safety from things nearly equal, but they have the advantage in lightness: they are easy for attacks and withdrawals, quicker at taking high ground, and by the use of the long sword they are ready to strike the Greek neck, getting the blow in before the close fight. They too have trained every art of fighting at close quarters, so that the experience is equal on both sides, and the advantage is the lightness of the dress.
So that the point of their spears may not be blunted, and so that they may not be broken against the Greek breastplates, they fitted a missile with skill and, pushing, pierced the scales.

So those who have always been beaten by the Greeks — the very men who have almost always beaten the Greeks — rarely beat them. The first cause is this: they do not rush at a run into the clash, so as not to leave the baggage behind; they are always shut up in the brick-shape of the army; and they go down on the knee, tiling the army with overlays of shields, in their eagerness to spend the Parthian missiles. This practice makes them both idle and unharmed, worn by sun and toil, while the barbarians come on in relays and withdraw again, resting by the interval-sendings of the nations. Further, no Roman fights by himself, nor does any become a champion fighting the mass in single combat.
translator_notes: Greek locked from PG 10 / Khazarzar Cesti 7.1 remainder after the Macedonian successors. Restorations <τὸ>, <τοῦτο>, <δ'>, <μὴ> are in the lock.
οἱ τοὺς Ἕλληνας σχεδὸν εἰπεῖν ἀεὶ νενικηκότες is kept as the Romans, who have almost always beaten Greeks, rarely beating those the Greeks always beat.

title: What the Roman kit still lacks against barbarians
english: Shots from a sling that hit the heads crush the helmet and go in; and it is hard to duck a missile in flight because of the piece of iron about the neck. Besides this they do not throw the javelins with aim, spending ten on one possible kill, and they do not meet charging horsemen with small pikes.

If then someone put a Greek breastplate and helmet on a Roman soldier, and gave him a longer pike, and taught each man to throw each of the spears at each mark and to fight on his own, and sometimes set a run so that the charge inside missile-range against the enemy would be sharp, no barbarian, being cut down, would hold out against the Romans.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.1 On arming. οὐκ ἂν βάρβαρος κοπτόμενος ἀρκέσειε Ῥωμαίοις: the barbarian would not suffice / hold out against Romans so equipped.

title: Do not make fortune mistress of the war
english: On the destruction of enemies. One must not fight the enemy in all things by close order and by battles, nor make fortune mistress of the whole of affairs. The end of war is unclear, and most things go contrary to expectation. Those better prepared in iron and men, or in bows and walls, have often been injured by wind, or sun, or place, or deceit, or a spectacle and an apparition; and in great wounds the daimon Pan is a constant.

The Phocians, better prepared in everything, did not receive the Thebans when they saw them crowned with laurel: the men who did not fear the war fled the crown. Wind and sun, meeting them in the face, more injured Flaminius and Paulus. The narrowness of the Gates made Leonidas equal to the five hundred myriads. Pan ran with the Athenians to Marathon against the Persians. Themistocles drove Xerxes from Greece by a lie.

Some smear missiles with drugs so that every wound becomes fatal; others set their strength in woods. Some, as they flee, destroy the pastures first; many poison the wells. Alexander took the Alans by farming hellebore. So one must not attempt those who stand against us from the open only, but must also general against the enemy by many hidden arts.

This old Carthaginian law has been thought out: they honored generals who planned the best things even if they did not succeed, and they punished those who attempted something rash and accomplished it, making the judgment not of fortune but of purpose. Fine too is the old iambic: the safe leader is more profitable to all than the rash.

The arts of generalship are very many, and there is nothing that happens that is not written down, to teach so that those things may not happen: healthy and well-watered camping-places, seizures of higher ground, ditching, advance-guards, night-marches, forward-rides, searches, ambushes, scouts, good arming, foraging, and with sleep a sufficient preparation; toward the enemy, distrust in all things.

As for exposing how they do harm, these things are clear, I think, and known to those who have kept company with histories: drinks of theriac as a defense against poisoned missiles, and the same cure for corrupted waters. Salt-drinkings we would decline for most, because of the disgust of taking them.
translator_notes: Opens Cesti 7.2. θέα μα καὶ φάσμα kept as spectacle and apparition (print split). Πάν is the god Pan, not a Bible name. No Scripture quotation in this slice.
πεντακοσίαις μυριάσιν: five hundred myriads (the Persian host at Thermopylae in this telling).

title: Starve them, and arm with air and water
english: If you cut the enemies' trees you will keep the other side from hiding. For not needing the others' pasture, the fodder brought along is enough, and whatever else has been thought out for a long campaign, toward having plenty of supplies and toward suffering nothing hard from the enemy — which is also the first deed of valor, because not to suffer is much better than to do harm. Pyrrhus, at any rate, though he had the advantage of the Romans, was consumed.

Time first, and wearing, and famine, and destruction, must especially be used against barbarians, whose gathering of the army is for a season and not a lasting force, but plunder from a raid. They bring foods measured in days and a stated number of missiles, and when those are spent their flight is obvious. Why then hurry to meet enemies whom, if I wait, I shall see driven by their own time-limit? Famine comes on them overdue, the few foods spent in vain. Come then, let us not even permit those starving men to flee. Let destruction without iron hold them, an end without battle. Let us beat them with air as ally and water as helper; with the elements let us arm against them. I general a secret array; I use a fight that does not show. Let every enemy fall when he has breathed, when he thirsts, or when he has eaten; I make all things dangerous to him. Let him starve if he stays, and take plague so that he may not flee. Let us do the work of a great prayer. Air as ally emptied Athens when it was filled with Lacedaemonians, and such a condition held the Carthaginians in Sicily. The victors dedicate such wars to their own gods. Let us too imitate those gods: automatic fortune comes about under our art.

Food, then, thus: let us make breads that will nourish the last day, from animals which are written down at the end, in pentagon 1, in which, along a line, are laid the signs of the Lydian mode being taken in besides — a defective zeta and an inverted tau. Shut both together into a vessel, sealing the lid with clay so that there may be no breathing-out for the beasts consumed inside by themselves; then grind their remains and put them into the water from which the cake is mixed. You will do the same if you smear the ovens with this juice; but for those who bake, this is a danger. [lacuna] Having prepared enough of such foods, furnish them to the enemies in whatever way you can.
translator_notes: Pentagon αʹ with Lydian-mode signs (defective zeta, inverted tau) is Africanus's cipher for the animals used in the bread; the names are not spelled in this lock. Print lacuna <.....> after κίνδυνος left unrestored.
This is a military-encyclopedia poison recipe in the lock; it is translated, not recommended.

title: Poisoned bread, poisoned wells, poisoned water
english: It would happen without suspicion if someone, being careless, worked the carrying toward an easy raid of the enemies and a wished-for snatching of the things brought to them, or if someone, feigning a serious flight, yielded to those coming on of the camp fortified with such foods. These do not bring a one-day death, nor do they kill the user at once. A plague-art overtakes this man and the one who did not eat; it is mixed into all and passes to the messmate. Into a house, a city, an army, a nation the plot migrates. Such a fate an Erinys procures for them. These are just dinners of penalties against barbarians, disease pouring upon all and an inexorable disaster overtaking the enemies.

If we fear we may use such a preparation in vain, either because they do not use it from suspicion, or because they have learned this from deserters, then, having feasted them, let us release either the criminals or the captives beside them; those who have kept company with them will take plague at once. I send them a plotting kindness. Let us likewise give them to drink such a loving-cup.

Three kinds of animals which lie in the second pentagon, toward the signs of the highest of the high — a turned-back gamma and an upright gamma: chop these so that all become ichor, and boiling them with very much water until all the fat of the boiled is consumed, pour into the enemies' watering-place. The bodies of those who have drunk will swell, themselves and the pack-animals; then a swelling with pain will stand upon them, and a man seeing himself become another from another, not recognizing the present form, slow both for flight and for an end, waiting the neighboring death, will pray for the speed of a warlike onset, that he may cease, both punished by the tension of inflammation and hated by himself because of the ugliness, the panoply that was inflated on the former body not holding the man now, so as to take from him even the pretense of standing in the arms.

Harm the waters also otherwise: fill the wells with dung and stones; and if the water is abundant, by fish-oil poured into them and by sea-purple, which for a long time make all water undrinkable. A greater standing of waters, or a lake, the myrtle-spurge thrown in will damage. Thus we shall first hinder the enemies by the drink. Let no one think the barbarians of the east unlearned in these things.
translator_notes: Second pentagon (turned-back gamma + upright gamma) again conceals animal names. [οἱ πολέμιοι] is a lock gloss on αὐτοῖς.
τιθύμαλλος μυρσινίτης: myrtle-spurge. θαλαττίᾳ πορφύρᾳ: murex / sea-purple.

title: Poisoned wine and poisoned air
english: They themselves often harm those who come against them. Poisoning of wine. Pharisees once prided themselves on having killed a phalanx of Romans by a pretense of flight. They were feasting, as it seemed, then withdrew when the others came on, leaving the meal ready. But the wine was a plot, poisoned with lime quenched in it. Wine is also poisoned with saltpeter-foam, box, hemlock, and like methods; for these, eaten, are enough to harm and to put enemies in a terrible state.

Since then we have taken foods and drinks as allies, come, let us also use air and wind against them. A man can guard himself from eating and drinking from enemies; how will he guard breath, how shut out air? Through these I come upon them.

Poisoning of air. The thrissos is a Thessalian snake, red in color, like a drakontis in length (and the same is also much in Asia; Syrians call it bathanerathan), which is written next in the third pentagon whose signs are of the parhypate of the high, a defective beta and an inverted gamma; and the lion is another snake, different, for it is both small and large, but the small is more takeable for this (and it too is much born in Syria). Let both be shut together into a vessel, safely very tight; and let the sharpest sun look at the vessel. When then they have been destroyed by one another and by the marsh-air and by time, let the vessel, set toward the wind accustomed to carry continuously toward those men, be opened, so that the exhalation from it may go to the opponents, the breeze ferrying into the breaths of those plotted against. Examples of the working: a horse running by will fall, and a neighboring man, and a bird not flying over comes down from the air murdered, caught by a wind faster than a fleeing wing.

If somewhere also against us, either by art of those from a plot, or also from one of the elements, destruction should happen, I have taken the treatment in advance for escape from the plague, having set it out in the skins before these. Themistocles, generaling, promised the victory against the Medes to himself by the sea-fight coming to be of men who would sail round by sleeplessness — this too being a great advantage over the enemies: to snatch their sleep.
translator_notes: Lock headings [Οἴνου φάρμαξις] and [Ἀέρος φάρμαξις] rendered as short labels. Φαρισαῖοι kept as the print; the military anecdote may not be the Jewish sect.
Syriac name βαθανηραθὰν and the two geographic asides are in lock brackets. Third pentagon conceals the snakes.

title: Steal their sleep at night
english: Old emperors of the Romans used the thing more nakedly and more actively, bringing on at night to the camp of the opponents both the lightest infantry and, with them, trumpeter-horsemen, through whom they accomplished one of two things: either, catching the advance-guards and watches more careless, they destroyed those in the way, or they threw in a panic. Some both shot and threw javelins, and those sent from a sling, whenever they missed, were carried against tent or horse or weapon: the noise accomplished more than wounding, always striking the neighbor with fear. The trumpeters, riding round, sounded the war-note, so as always to furnish to those stationed at that point the impression that the enemies would fall on at any moment.

Then after day they led the camp out, by every means contriving not to join battle, and setting out the coming night like the one past, their own men resting with all leisure of day, or by the sending of others, and the same men always being plotted against to stay sleepless. Who does not know how unmanageable the things from this are? Pain of the head, bad eating, slackness of body from desire to sleep even somehow, the same condition succeeding night and day. Having done this next, we shall take the opponents at the first shout, made womanish by sleeplessness.
translator_notes: Closes Cesti 7.2. πανικὸν is panic (the Pan-fright of the previous chapter), not a Bible term. τεθηλυμμένους: made womanish / unmanned by sleeplessness.

title: The cock-stone and the athlete’s meal
english: Athletic contest. All those skilled in these things praise the stones found in the bellies of noble cocks as co-workers of virtue and victory. Worn either in leather, or carried under the tongue, they keep soldiers and athletes and gladiators well set, lasting, and not thirsty. Others tell another form and color of them: some crystal-like and rough, some black — those who speak truly. They are found in the winner when he is cut up, as if not the virtue of the bird but the nature of the stone had become the cause of prevailing.

Since then, whether worn under the mouth or about the arm, the stone either falls out or is cut round by an antagonist, one must use an unsuspected wrapping of much power. Let the cock that has won, prepared as is the custom, be eaten whole by the contestant, so that the flesh is stripped, all of it, and the bones kept whole and unbroken; then after the table let it be purified by fire. The bird, no longer of day but a messenger of victory that will be, making the eater successor of its own unbeatenness, migrates into the man as by virtue.

The son of Neocles used the stone and the food when fighting the Persians; and from there he legislated the cock-fights in Athens when it had been raised, and the Athenians after the Median victory led a victory-feast of cocks.
translator_notes: Cesti 7.3. ὁ Νεοκλέους is Themistocles. κατατυθέντι τῷ νικήσαντι: the winning cock cut up, not a human victor.
